  • availability-payment-unspecified
  • demand-sensitivity-unquantified
  • private-finance-structure-incomplete

6.6.C Mitigation

By Month 9 (2027-07-12), commission an independent demand forecast and sensitivity analysis covering passenger demand (±20%, ±30%), freight uplift scenarios, and fare elasticity. Model DSCR under low-demand cases and define minimum-revenue thresholds (e.g., EUR 180 million/year at 2.5 million passengers) that trigger renegotiation or subsidy top-up. By Month 12 (2027-10-12), secure binding availability-payment commitments from Spain, Morocco and EU specifying: total annual amount (estimated EUR 230–284 million/year, escalated annually); duration (30 years, aligned with debt maturity); triggering conditions (e.g., if actual revenues fall <EUR 200 million/year, availability payments increase to close the gap); and parliamentary/budget backing (not discretionary). Design the rail-systems concession with explicit demand-risk caps (e.g., if revenues fall >30%, operator can trigger cost-sharing or operational optimization review). Reduce the private debt tranche from EUR 4.4 billion to EUR 2–3 billion (shift more civil works to public balance sheet) if availability-payment commitments cannot be locked in by Month 15 (2028-01-12).

6.6.D Consequence

Without explicit, binding availability-payment agreements in place by Month 15 (2028-01-12), the private finance structure will collapse at the lender-commitment stage (Month 24–30 = 2028-10-12 to 2029-04-12), forcing a rapid pivot to a fully public or mixed-capital structure. This will trigger a 6–12 month funding redesign and potentially require both states to absorb the EUR 4.4 billion private debt directly, increasing public-sector borrowing and jeopardizing EU/multilateral co-financing approval. Alternatively, if availability payments are discretionary (not backed by law), demand shortfalls will trigger mid-programme liquidity crises requiring emergency tranches or operational scaling-back.

6.6.E Root Cause

The plan assumes the private rail-systems finance model is attractive to equity and debt investors, but the DSCR gap (0.15x vs 1.0x required) is too large for a private investor to underwrite, and the plan has not established that sovereign availability-payment commitments exist or are credible. This is a classical megaproject error: the finance structure is designed on the assumption that revenue will cover debt, and public support is treated as a residual backstop rather than a planned, funded, and binding commitment from the outset. No European high-speed rail crossing has been financed on private terms alone; the plan must specify the public commitment upfront or shift to a public or public-private joint-venture capital structure.

7.4.A Issue - Depth assumption unverified and core concept cost exposure unmanaged.

The plan states 100 m anchoring depth but published Strait bathymetry shows several hundred metres to ~900 m. This 800 m variance is not a data-gathering nuance—it is a fundamental structural uncertainty that invalidates early cost estimates and forces a redesign of the support concept once seabed works begin, at which point reversal is impossible. A pillar-only fallback adds EUR 4–8 billion and 12–36 months. The SWOT and scenarios acknowledge this but do not enforce a hard stop on casting-yard commitment until seabed verification is complete. The contingency reserve of EUR 7.2 billion is insufficient to cover this range, and no cost-control authority is in place to declare when overrun exposure exceeds acceptable thresholds.

7.4.C Mitigation

Enforce a hard release gate at Month 24 (2028-10-12): casting-yard construction advance (EUR 2–5 billion) is released only if the seabed campaign (geophysics by Month 6 = 2027-04-12, borings by Month 12 = 2027-10-12, independent review by Month 18 = 2028-04-12) concludes with an acceptable design basis and support-concept freeze signed off by the binational Board and the Lead Certifier. If the campaign reveals unreconcilable depth or geology conflicts, trigger a formal concept-change decision process: compare pillar-only, tether-only and hybrid costs and schedule impact against the envelope; take a new funding decision or descope. Establish the independent Project Cost Authority by Month 2 (2026-12-12) with explicit authority to halt tranche release if residual concept-redesign exposure exceeds 15% of the contingency pool (EUR 1.08 billion). Document this trigger in the governance charter signed at treaty ratification.

7.4.D Consequence

Without this gate enforcement, EUR 2–5 billion is committed to casting yards by Month 24 (2028-10-12) before the seabed campaign reports. If redesign is then needed, the sunk investment biases decision-making toward a wrong concept to justify the spend. Cost overruns of EUR 4–8 billion (pillar fallback) exceed the EUR 7.2 billion reserve by EUR 0.8–4.8 billion, consuming 56–111% of the reserve and leaving no buffer for any other risk (schedule slip, supply-chain inflation, environmental injunctions). The 20-year horizon becomes unachievable without sovereign-guarantee escalation or scope cuts that devalue the connection benefit.

7.4.E Root Cause

The initial plan's pillar-supported 100 m premise was not validated against hydrographic survey data before being locked into the envelope and timeline. The plan document and scenarios acknowledge the conflict but treat it as a research finding rather than a gating factor. No trigger rule prevents casting-yard advance (EUR 2–5 billion) from being released at Month 24 (2028-10-12) if the seabed campaign has not concluded, and no named authority is empowered to halt spending if support-concept redesign risk exceeds the contingency pool.

7.6.A Issue - Contingency reserve is insufficient for plausible cost overrun; funding gap is unassigned.

The plan allocates EUR 7.2 billion (18% of envelope) as contingency. Cost overrun exposure is estimated at EUR 10–18 billion (25–45%), creating an unfunded gap of EUR 2.8–10.8 billion. The plan notes this gap in the canonical facts but does not assign funding responsibility or declare a trigger for a new funding decision. Within the EUR 7.2 billion contingency, the plan earmarks EUR 0.25–0.4 billion for ecological mitigation, leaving EUR 6.8–6.95 billion available. It also reserves EUR 1–2 billion for geotechnical surprises (the Design Change Reserve), leaving EUR 4.8–5.95 billion unearmarked after carving out earmarks. A pillar-only concept fallback alone (EUR 4–8 billion) consumes 56–111% of the EUR 7.2 billion gross reserve, with the upper end exceeding available funds. No independent cost authority is named to escalate overrun exposure, and no trigger rule declares when a new funding decision is required.

7.6.D Consequence

Without a named Cost Authority and overrun thresholds, cost variance accumulates invisibly across multiple tranches. By Month 60 (2031-10-12) or Month 72 (2032-10-12), when 50% of spending has occurred, a EUR 4–8 billion cost overrun is discovered (support-concept redesign, supply inflation, immersion delays compounded). At that point, the reserve is exhausted and the project must choose between scope reduction (abandoning shallow-section tethers, shortening crossing to 10 km, phased opening), mid-stream financing escalation (triggering additional sovereign guarantees, private-debt restructuring), or schedule delay (pushing completion to Month 252 or later, beyond the user constraint). Each option undermines the commercial case, lender confidence and political credibility. A timely cost decision at Month 6 (2027-04-12) or Month 18 (2028-04-12) allows scope or funding adjustment before irreversible commitments; delayed discovery creates crisis-driven decisions.

7.6.E Root Cause

The EUR 40 billion envelope and EUR 7.2 billion contingency were set before seabed data were available to ground cost estimates. First-of-kind marine-construction projects (HZMB, Fehmarnbelt, immersed tubes) routinely experience 25–45% cost growth from design to completion. The plan does not align contingency sizing to the sources of uncertainty: support-concept redesign, supply-chain inflation over 20 years, immersion delays from weather and contractor scarcity, and design-code development cost. No named authority (Project Cost Authority) is empowered to declare when variance against budget exceeds thresholds and triggers new funding decisions. Tranches are gated but funding sources for overruns are not specified.

8.4.A Issue - Contingency reserve is structurally insufficient and underestimates first-of-kind marine-construction cost risk

The plan allocates EUR 7.2 billion (18% of envelope) contingency against plausible cumulative overruns of EUR 10–18 billion (25–45%), leaving an unfunded gap of EUR 2.8–10.8 billion. For megaprojects, EU/multilateral practice flags overruns of 20–30% as normal; first-of-kind marine structures with no design code compound this by 15–25 percentage points. The support-concept fallback alone (pillar-only redesign if seabed data prove tethers infeasible) consumes EUR 4–8 billion and 12–36 months, exhausting 56–111% of the reserve. Simultaneously, ecological mitigation (EUR 250–400 million), egress and hardening infrastructure (EUR 0.5–3 billion), and shipping-security passive covers (EUR 0.5–1 billion) are carving into the contingency rather than sitting above it. The EUR 40 billion hard cap creates a binary outcome: either overrun is absorbed within the reserve (leaving no margin for concurrent risks), or the project faces scope cuts, schedule compression, or a mid-programme funding crisis and sovereign guarantee escalation.

Run 10,000 iterations; extract P50, P80 and P95 outcomes. For the 'largest cost driver' (support concept), run three scenarios (pillar-dominated, hybrid, tether-dominated) with independent cost and probability estimates; treat support-concept selection as a decision that reduces cost variance, not a binary bet. Establish a tiered contingency structure: (a) Design Change Reserve (EUR 1–2 billion for foundation surprises, accessible at gates Month 9, 18, 30, 42 = 2027-07-12, 2028-04-12, 2029-04-12, 2030-04-12); (b) Overrun Reserve (EUR 4–5 billion for cost growth within the structural, material and schedule bands); (c) Tail-Risk Reserve (EUR 2–3 billion for low-probability, high-impact events: major seismic event during construction, multiple joint failures, cascading supply-chain collapse). Price each tranche by risk type and fund them separately under lender/insurance covenants. By Month 3 (2027-01-12), present a new funding decision to both treasuries quantifying the EUR 2.8–10.8 billion gap and proposing closure via (i) demand-upside hedging (revenue risk transfer), (ii) availability-payment escalation, or (iii) scope phasing. Do not proceed to Month 6 (2027-04-12) design gates until the gap is funded.

8.4.D Consequence

Without this fix, the project faces a 30–50% probability of a mid-programme funding crisis at Months 48–72 (2030-10-12 to 2032-10-12) when casting-yard ramp-up and immersion reveal true cost-per-km performance. At that point, the EUR 7.2 billion reserve will have absorbed design-change surprises, material inflation and contractor day-rate escalation, leaving little buffer for a major geotechnical or immersion redesign. The project will be forced to (1) cut scope mid-construction (eliminate one tube, reduce immersion pace, defer egress infrastructure), (2) compress schedule (reduce immersion weather-window margin, accept 1–2 year delay to service opening and revenue), or (3) escalate sovereign guarantees (both states underwrite overruns above the cap, a political liability and treaty-violation risk if one state declines). Lenders and insurers will demand additional covenants (debt-to-capital ratios, take-or-pay guarantees for availability payments) that effectively nationalize the asset and erode private-sector participation. The insurance market will refuse to quote fatigue and sabotage risk without a funded cost-certainty commitment, delaying opening insurance proof-of-insurability to Month 96+ (2034-10-12+), dangerously late for an asset approaching service opening.

8.4.E Root Cause

The plan treats contingency as a percentage-of-budget rule (18%) rather than a risk-based allocation tied to probability-weighted cost outcomes. First-of-kind marine-structure cost risk is not priced using Monte Carlo simulation, actuarial analogy to comparable megaprojects (Fehmarnbelt, HZMB, immersed tubes, offshore wind), or parametric cost-per-km escalation models. The hybrid support concept and seabed uncertainty are acknowledged as 'largest cost driver' but no sensitivity analysis quantifies their tail-risk distribution. The plan also fails to segregate insurable vs uninsurable cost drivers: fatigue, sabotage and marine-delay cost escalation (insurance-driven) cannot be pooled with geotechnical foundation redesign or inflation (balance-sheet driven). A 20-year, fixed-price megaproject with unresolved depth and geology is inherently tail-risk-heavy; the contingency reflects a nominal 'base case' rather than P50/P80 cost certainty.

8.5.A Issue - Binational governance structure lacks binding enforcement of decision authority, creating 3–6 month consensus cycles that jeopardize the 20-year horizon

The plan specifies a 'treaty-backed binational coordinating commission with Board tie-break and single lead certifier' but does not codify the decision authority, escalation path or consequence of deadlock. The 'delegated approval thresholds' (CEO <2%, Board 2–5%, >5% triggers political review) are proposed, not binding; no treaty language, parliamentary statute or operating agreement is quoted. The 'Month 24 (2028-10-12) stop rule' (no main-construction tranche if treaty not ratified) is stated but assumes both parliaments will ratify on time—a weak assumption given that cross-border infrastructure treaties routinely slip 12–24 months (Fehmarnbelt took 23 years negotiation, HZMB took 10 years, Gotthard took 18 years parliamentary phases). The plan also does not specify who decides on design changes when Spain and Morocco disagree (e.g., egress refuge siting at the Spanish landfall vs the Moroccan landfall; shipping-corridor width; seismic design case), or what happens if the Lead Certifier and the Binational Board reach conflicting conclusions on safety-case adequacy. Historical precedent (HZMB, Fehmarnbelt) shows that unresolved design-change decisions absorb 3–6 months per cycle, and major certification disputes (e.g., differing seismic codes or fatigue-life methods) can stall approval for 12–18 months. A 20-year schedule with tight immersion weather windows cannot absorb ten 3–6 month consensus cycles.

8.5.B Tags

  • governance-deadlock
  • consensus-cycle-delay
  • decision-authority-gap
  • treaty-ratification-risk
  • certifier-conflict-unresolved

8.5.C Mitigation

By Month 1 (2026-11-12), establish a joint Spanish–Moroccan treaty negotiation team with explicit mandate from both transport and finance ministers; hire a law firm experienced in cross-border megaproject treaties (precedents: Fehmarnbelt, HZMB, Channel Tunnel) to draft a negotiation roadmap identifying the seven critical articles: (1) legal personality and liability of the binational authority; (2) Board composition, voting rules and tie-break mechanism (recommend independent technical director with casting vote, or automatic escalation to foreign ministries within 30 days if tie persists); (3) delegated approval authority with thresholds in euros and timeline (e.g., CEO approves design changes <EUR 50 million and <3 months schedule impact within 1 week; Board within 4 weeks for EUR 50–200 million; >EUR 200 million goes to political level within 30 days); (4) procurement rules harmonizing EU and Moroccan law; (5) safety and certification: single Lead Certifier with explicit power to issue conditional approval pending remediation, and Board must implement or appeal within 30 days to political level; (6) dispute resolution (international arbitration, not national courts); (7) treaty amendment and withdrawal rules (12-month notice, binding negotiation period). By Month 6 (2027-04-12), complete draft treaty and present for ministerial signature; target parliamentary ratification by Month 12 (2027-10-12), with a firm Month 24 (2028-10-12) stop rule: if ratification slips beyond Month 24 (2028-10-12), automatically suspend all main-construction commitments (casting yards, immersion contracts) and trigger a political review on scope/schedule/structure. Establish a Design Change Control Board within the authority with Spanish, Moroccan and Lead Certifier representatives; publish decision criteria and timelines (15 days for routine technical approvals, 30 days for major changes); any decision not made within the timeline defaults to the most conservative option (e.g., if egress refuge siting is disputed, default to dual refuges at both landfalls, cost absorbed within Design Change Reserve). Model the decision-cycle timeline (Month 1 = 2026-11-12 to Month 30 = 2029-04-12 showing all 15 gates/reviews with decision authority and consequence of deadlock) and present it to both parliaments during ratification as evidence of schedule protection.

8.5.D Consequence

Without this fix, the project will experience 2–4 rounds of 3–6 month consensus-building cycles in the Months 6–48 (2027-04-12 to 2030-10-12) window when design and permitting decisions accumulate (support-concept freeze, certification gates, egress design, shipping-corridor definition, foundational joint standards). By Month 48 (2030-10-12), accumulated consensus delays will have slipped the critical path by 6–12 months, narrowing the immersion-window margin from 6 months to near-zero. Casting yards will have ramped up on a design baseline that later requires change-orders (estimated 1–3 per yard per year); change-order processing (dispute resolution, cost negotiation, schedule impact assessment) will take 6–8 weeks each under the current governance, consuming additional critical-path buffer. The Lead Certifier's Month 42 (2030-04-12) certification gate will face unresolved design disputes (e.g., seismic load case methodology if Spain and Morocco interpret EN 1998 differently, or fatigue-life assessment if the certifier and Board disagree on allowable stress ranges), delaying final design approval by 3–6 months and forcing fabrication to proceed under conditional approval—a high-risk state for an insurance underwriter and lender. Treaty ratification failure (if slipped beyond Month 24 = 2028-10-12) will trigger the stop rule and force scope reduction or schedule re-planning at Month 24–30 (2028-10-12 to 2029-04-12), by which time EUR 2–4 billion will have been committed to casting-yard site prep and supply-chain mobilization, stranding costs and reducing political flexibility. Insurers will refuse to quote coverage for cost overrun, delay-in-opening or third-party liability until governance is legally ratified and operationalized, delaying proof-of-insurability to Month 48–60 (2030-10-12 to 2031-10-12), a critical juncture when fabrication is ramping and design changes are most expensive.

8.5.E Root Cause

The plan treats the binational delivery vehicle as a 'decision' that is already made, without drafting the legal instruments (treaty text, concession agreement, procurement rules, design-change authority schedule) that would operationalize it. The 'Month 12 (2027-10-12) target' for treaty ratification is aggressive for two parliaments (Spain's parliament and Morocco's parliament and any EU Council alignment required); no negotiation team budget, staffing, timeline or pre-negotiation consensus-building is budgeted. The Lead Certifier role is appointed at Month 6 (2027-04-12) but has no authority over the Board, no mechanism to force a design-change decision if the Board is deadlocked, and no liability or enforcement power if the Board ignores their certification condition. The plan also fails to define what 'single technical regulator' means in practice: does it override Spanish and Moroccan national maritime and railway authorities, or does it merely coordinate them? If it merely coordinates, then design disputes default back to dual national review, recreating the consensus cycle. The plan's 'Governance is realistic' claim in the Scenarios section is not supported by treaty text or legal analysis.

8.6.A Issue - Debt-service gap and revenue model are structurally unachievable, requiring an unsustainable availability-payment commitment that masks operational insolvency

The plan allocates EUR 8.8 billion to rail systems and operations, financed by private debt (EUR 4.4 billion at 4.5%, implying ~EUR 270 million/year debt service) and private equity. Opening-day planning-case revenue is EUR 240 million/year (4.0 million passengers at EUR 60 per trip); annual operations and maintenance EUR 200 million/year (estimate). This yields an operating surplus of EUR 40 million/year, implying a debt-service-coverage ratio (DSCR) of only 0.15x—far below the 1.2x–1.5x required by commercial lenders and the 1.0x+ minimum acceptable to European development banks. The shortfall (EUR 230 million/year to reach 1.0x DSCR) must be bridged by 'availability payments from the states/EU,' but the plan does not quantify the total public subsidy, specify which entity commits it, define how long it runs, or analyze what happens if demand falls 20–30% below the planning case (a plausible tail scenario for a novel, high-price-point service). The plan assumes EUR 100–150 million/year freight and vehicle-shuttle revenue in the 'forecast case' but excludes it from the 'planning case,' reducing transparency. It also does not account for inflation of the EUR 200 million/year opex baseline over a 20+ year service life (2% annual increase = EUR 600 million cumulative by Year 50). The private-debt tranche (EUR 4.4 billion) cannot be syndicated or refinanced without an ironclad availability-payment covenant backed by the sovereign treasuries; this de facto nationalizes the asset risk while appearing to transfer it to private capital.

8.6.B Tags

  • revenue-insufficient
  • dscr-unsustainable
  • subsidy-uncapped
  • demand-downside-unpriced
  • private-debt-illusion

8.6.C Mitigation

By Month 3 (2027-01-12), commission an independent demand study from a transport-modeling firm (precedent: Steer Davies Gleave, Arup) covering (1) demand sensitivity to price (elasticity of –0.5 to –0.8, typical for rail); (2) through-running adoption (share of Spanish and Moroccan rail traffic able to flow through-train without transfer); (3) freight potential (truck and rail freight, especially agricultural exports from Morocco and imports to Spain); (4) base-case, upside and downside scenarios across a 20-year horizon. Run three scenarios: (a) planning case (4.0 million passengers + EUR 100 million freight/year at opening); (b) downside (2.5 million passengers + EUR 40 million freight/year, reflecting 40% demand miss and lower freight uptake); (c) upside (6.0 million passengers + EUR 150 million freight). Model DSCR for each under the assumed debt structure (EUR 4.4 billion private debt at 4.5%). If the downside scenario yields DSCR <0.8x, escalate to the finance ministries of both countries with a new funding decision: either (i) increase public equity in the rail-systems tranche (convert some private debt to public capital, reducing debt service), (ii) commit to a formal availability-payment covenant guaranteeing minimum revenue of EUR 270 million/year for the first 15 years, with a sunset clause allowing for upward price adjustment if demand exceeds forecasts, or (iii) reduce the rail-systems scope (defer non-core rail investments, focus on core tunnel and approach connections). Document the availability-payment commitment as a binding sovereign guarantee with a 'deep pockets' clause: the commitment is not discharged if toll revenue falls below the threshold due to demand shortfall or cost increases, and the shortfall is immediately payable by the issuing state on demand. By Month 12 (2027-10-12), negotiate anchor-tenant agreements with Spanish and Moroccan rail operators that commit them to a minimum throughput (e.g., 3.0 million passengers/year within 5 years of opening) in exchange for toll discounts or preferential scheduling; these agreements operationalize demand risk by making the operators liable for shortfalls. Price demand risk into the private-debt syndication: require a 25–35% equity cushion in the rail-systems tranche (increase private equity to EUR 5.5–6.0 billion, reduce private debt to EUR 2.8–3.3 billion) to absorb a 30% demand miss without triggering a covenant breach. This rebalancing is likely to render the rail-systems tranche unattractive to private investors without substantial public subsidy, making the true cost of the availability-payment model explicit. If the availability-payment commitment exceeds EUR 200 million/year, flag it to both finance ministries as a contingent liability that must be approved by their treasuries and parliaments, not buried in the project sponsor's budget.

8.6.D Consequence

Without this fix, the project will face a debt-refinancing crisis at Months 60–84 (2031-10-12 to 2033-10-12) when opening approaches and private lenders demand to see proof of demand and cost assumptions. If actual demand in the first 2–3 years of operation (Months 132–156 = 2037-10-12 to 2040-01-12) falls 20–30% below forecast, the DSCR will drop to 0.10–0.12x and breach all debt covenants. At that point, the private lenders will demand either (a) a takeover by the issuing sovereigns (converting debt to government bonds or equity), (b) a formal government guarantee on the shortfall (monetizing availability payments retroactively), or (c) debt restructuring (extending maturity, reducing coupon). Each outcome converts the nominally 'private' rail-systems tranche into a public liability and erodes confidence in the project's financial model. Insurers will demand proof of demand-risk mitigation before issuing opening insurance for operational liability, third-party liability and business-interruption cover; if the DSCR is structurally <1.0x, insurers will either decline coverage or impose a 15–25% premium loading for 'enterprise-risk uncertainty,' raising effective insurance cost by EUR 20–40 million/year and further straining the revenue model. By Month 108 (2035-10-12), six months before opening, the project will face a 'do-or-die' decision: either both governments formally guarantee availability payments (a treaty amendment or supplemental agreement, taking 3–6 months to negotiate and ratify) or the private investors walk away and the asset defaults into public ownership, triggering a political crisis in both countries. The 6-month window to opening is too late to secure either outcome without imposing schedule pressure (compress commissioning timelines, defer safety testing) that increases operational risk. A transparent, early availability-payment commitment (by Month 3–6 = 2027-01-12 to 2027-04-12) would allow the debt syndication to proceed on known terms and give private investors confidence; deferring this decision to Month 60+ (2031-10-12+) guarantees a refinancing crisis.

8.6.E Root Cause

The plan conflates civil-works capital (EUR 24.0 billion) with rail systems and operations (EUR 8.8 billion) and treats them as a unified EUR 40 billion envelope, obscuring the fact that the rail-operations component is separately financed and has its own revenue model. The revenue forecast (4.0 million passengers/year at opening, 5–6 million by Year 5–10) is stated as a 'planning case' but is not anchored to an independent demand study, market-sizing analysis, or sensitivity testing. For novel infrastructure (Gotthard, Channel Tunnel, HZMB early operations), demand often undershoots initial forecasts by 15–40% in the first 3–5 years. The plan does not model a conservative demand scenario (e.g., 2.5–3.0 million passengers/year, reflecting caution on through-running adoption and price sensitivity). The EUR 60 per-trip fare is stated as an 'estimate' but is not benchmarked against competing routes (flights Malaga–Tangier, EUR 80–120; ferries, EUR 10–40; road transport, EUR 5–15); if the tunnel must compete on price, revenue per trip may be EUR 40–50, reducing opening-day fare revenue to EUR 160–200 million/year and deepening the DSCR shortfall to 0.08–0.10x. The plan also assumes that 'availability payments' (effectively a take-or-pay subsidy from the Spanish and Moroccan treasuries) will cover the gap for 30 years, but does not specify the total public commitment (estimated EUR 230 million/year × 30 years = EUR 6.9 billion present value at 3% discount) or how this obligation will be reconciled against other transport-investment priorities in both countries.
